subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A surgeon examines two resected specimens. The first is a small outpouching of the terminal ileum in a child that, on histology, contains mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, and serosa. The second is a sigmoid outpouching in an adult that contains only mucosa and submucosa, with the muscularis externa absent from the wall of the pouch.
question: Which of the following best characterizes the first (ileal) lesion?

options.text: A false diverticulum composed of mucosa and submucosa only
A true diverticulum in which all layers of the gut wall outpouch
A pseudodiverticulum where vasa recta penetrate the muscularis externa
An acquired diverticulum caused by increased intraluminal pressure
A diverticulum lacking a muscularis externa and serosa

explanation_correct: A true diverticulum is defined by outpouching of all layers of the gut wall, and Meckel diverticulum is the classic example. The specimen described contains mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, and serosa, so it is a true diverticulum. This contrasts with acquired (false) diverticula, in which only mucosa and submucosa herniate through a defect in the muscularis, typically where vasa recta penetrate the muscle layer.

explanation_incorrect.A: Mucosa and submucosa alone describe a false diverticulum (pseudodiverticulum), such as a colonic diverticulum, not a lesion containing all wall layers.
explanation_incorrect.C: Herniation where vasa recta penetrate the muscularis externa is the mechanism of acquired false diverticula (eg, Zenker and colonic diverticula), not a true diverticulum.
explanation_incorrect.D: Increased intraluminal pressure with focal wall weakness produces acquired false diverticula such as diverticulosis; a true diverticulum is a congenital, full-thickness outpouching.
explanation_incorrect.E: A lesion lacking muscularis externa and serosa is by definition a false diverticulum, which is the opposite of what the histology of this specimen shows.

educationalObjective: A true diverticulum (eg, Meckel) contains all layers of the gut wall, whereas false diverticula contain only mucosa and submucosa.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 68-year-old man with obesity and a long history of a low-fiber diet high in red meat undergoes screening colonoscopy, which reveals multiple outpouchings clustered in the sigmoid colon. He is asymptomatic. His brother, who has a high-fiber diet, has no such findings.
question: Which of the following best explains the development of this patient's colonic outpouchings?

options.text: Failure of neural crest cell migration to the distal colon
Persistence of the vitelline duct with ectopic gastric mucosa
Transmural inflammation with crypt abscesses confined to the colon
Increased intraluminal pressure and focal weakness of the colonic wall
Ischemic necrosis at a colonic watershed area

explanation_correct: This patient has diverticulosis: multiple acquired false diverticula of the colon, classically in the sigmoid. It arises from increased intraluminal pressure combined with focal weakness in the colonic wall, where vasa recta penetrate the muscularis externa. It is common (about 50% of people older than 60) and is associated with obesity and diets low in fiber but high in total fat and red meat; it is often asymptomatic.

explanation_incorrect.A: Failed neural crest migration causes Hirschsprung disease (aganglionic megacolon), not acquired colonic diverticula.
explanation_incorrect.B: A persistent vitelline duct with ectopic gastric mucosa describes Meckel diverticulum, a congenital true diverticulum of the ileum, not sigmoid false diverticula.
explanation_incorrect.C: Transmural inflammation with crypt abscesses suggests inflammatory bowel disease, which is not the mechanism of uncomplicated diverticulosis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Ischemic necrosis at a watershed (splenic flexure or rectosigmoid junction) describes colonic ischemia, not the pressure-related outpouchings of diverticulosis.

educationalObjective: Diverticulosis is common sigmoid false diverticula caused by increased intraluminal pressure and focal wall weakness, associated with low-fiber, high-fat/red-meat diets and obesity.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 72-year-old woman with known sigmoid diverticulosis suddenly passes a large amount of bright red blood per rectum. She has no abdominal pain, fever, or tenderness. Her vital signs are stable, and her abdomen is soft and nontender. Laboratory studies show a normal leukocyte count.
question: Which of the following is the most likely source of this patient's bleeding?

options.text: Rupture of a vasa recta vessel in a colonic false diverticulum
Inflammation and wall thickening of a diverticulum
A colovesical fistula between the sigmoid colon and bladder
Ischemic necrosis at the splenic flexure watershed
Tortuous dilated vessels in the right-sided colon

explanation_correct: Painless hematochezia in a patient with diverticulosis is diverticular bleeding. The false diverticula form where vasa recta penetrate the muscularis externa, and the thin-walled vessel can rupture into the pouch, producing painless bright red blood. The absence of pain, fever, and leukocytosis argues against diverticulitis, in which hematochezia is actually rare.

explanation_incorrect.B: Inflammation with wall thickening is diverticulitis, which causes LLQ pain, fever, and leukocytosis; hematochezia is rare in diverticulitis and this patient is painless.
explanation_incorrect.C: A colovesical fistula is a complication of diverticulitis and causes pneumaturia (air in urine), not isolated painless rectal bleeding.
explanation_incorrect.D: Colonic ischemia at the splenic flexure causes crampy abdominal pain followed by hematochezia in older adults, not painless bleeding in a patient with known diverticulosis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Angiodysplasia causes painless hematochezia but arises from tortuous dilated vessels most often in the right colon, typically in older patients with associations such as aortic stenosis or von Willebrand disease.

educationalObjective: Diverticulosis commonly causes painless hematochezia from vasa recta rupture; diverticulitis causes LLQ pain, fever, and leukocytosis with rare bleeding.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 64-year-old man with a history of diverticulosis presents with 3 days of left lower quadrant pain, fever, and leukocytosis. CT shows a thickened, inflamed sigmoid colon with a pericolic fluid collection. He then develops pneumaturia: air is passed in the urine during voiding, with no history of urinary tract instrumentation.
question: Which of the following complications best accounts for this new finding?

options.text: Inflammatory stenosis causing large bowel obstruction
Perforation with generalized peritonitis
A colovesical fistula between the sigmoid colon and the bladder
Rupture of a vasa recta causing painless hematochezia
Formation of a pericolic abscess without organ involvement

explanation_correct: This patient has diverticulitis and has developed pneumaturia, the classic sign of a colovesical fistula between the inflamed sigmoid colon and the bladder. Fistula formation is a recognized complication of diverticulitis; air and fecal material can pass into the urinary tract, causing air in the urine. Other complications include abscess, obstruction from inflammatory stenosis, and perforation with peritonitis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Inflammatory stenosis causes obstruction with distention and obstipation, not air in the urine.
explanation_incorrect.B: Perforation leads to peritonitis with severe diffuse pain and guarding, not isolated pneumaturia.
explanation_incorrect.D: Vasa recta rupture causes painless hematochezia, a feature of diverticulosis rather than this fistulous complication of diverticulitis.
explanation_incorrect.E: A pericolic abscess is a localized pus collection indicated by the fluid collection and fever, but it does not by itself explain air passing in the urine.

educationalObjective: Pneumaturia in a patient with diverticulitis signals a colovesical fistula, a complication distinct from abscess, obstruction, and perforation.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 58-year-old woman presents with left lower quadrant pain, fever, and a leukocyte count of 15,000/µL. Imaging shows wall thickening around a sigmoid diverticulum with no abscess, fistula, obstruction, or free air. She is otherwise stable and tolerating a diet.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient's condition?

options.text: Urgent surgical resection with a colostomy
Long-term antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent recurrence
Angiographic embolization of a bleeding vasa recta
Immediate colonoscopic decompression of the sigmoid colon
Supportive care alone, without antibiotics

explanation_correct: This patient has uncomplicated diverticulitis: inflamed diverticula with wall thickening causing LLQ pain, fever, and leukocytosis, but without abscess, fistula, obstruction, or perforation. Uncomplicated diverticulitis is treated with supportive care, while complicated diverticulitis warrants antibiotics (and sometimes intervention). The absence of any complication here makes conservative supportive management appropriate.

explanation_incorrect.A: Urgent resection with colostomy is reserved for complicated disease such as perforation with peritonitis, not uncomplicated diverticulitis.
explanation_incorrect.B: Antibiotics are indicated for complicated diverticulitis, not as long-term prophylaxis in uncomplicated cases managed supportively.
explanation_incorrect.C: Angiographic embolization treats diverticular bleeding from a vasa recta; this patient has no hematochezia, and bleeding is rare in diverticulitis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Colonoscopic decompression is used for colonic pseudo-obstruction or volvulus, not for localized sigmoid diverticulitis without obstruction.

educationalObjective: Uncomplicated diverticulitis is managed with supportive care; antibiotics are added for complicated disease (abscess, fistula, obstruction, perforation).
